claim: Skilled performance is characterized by precise and flexible control of movement sequences in space and time.
source: Skilled performance is characterized by precise and flexible control of movement sequences in space and time.
evidence: This is a general statement about skilled performance presented in the abstract without specific experimental support in this sentence.

claim: Recent theories suggest that integrated spatio-temporal trajectories are generated by intrinsic dynamics of motor and premotor networks.
source: Recent theories suggest that integrated spatio-temporal trajectories are generated by intrinsic dynamics of motor and premotor networks.
evidence: This claim references recent theories without specific citations in this sentence, drawing on established theoretical frameworks.

claim: Behavioural advantages emerge when a trained spatial or temporal feature of sequences is transferred to a new spatio-temporal combination.
source: This contrasts with behavioural advantages that emerge when a trained spatial or temporal feature of sequences is transferred to a new spatio-temporal combination arguing for independent neural representations of these sequence features.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral results presented in the manuscript showing transfer effects.

claim: Only the contralateral primary motor cortex exhibited unique patterns for each spatio-temporal sequence combination.
source: whereas only the contralateral primary motor cortex exhibited unique patterns for each spatio-temporal sequence combination
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the fMRI pattern classification results showing integrated encoding in contralateral M1.

claim: Bilateral premotor areas represented spatial and temporal features independently of each other.
source: bilateral premotor areas represented spatial and temporal features independently of each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI classification analysis showing independent spatial and temporal encoding in premotor areas.

claim: The ordering of muscle activations is referred to as the 'spatial feature' of a sequence.
source: The ordering of these muscle activations—and hence the ordering of the movements of different body parts in space—is here referred to as the 'spatial feature' of a sequence.
evidence: This is a definitional claim establishing terminology used in the study.

claim: Movement sequences are often characterized by a stereotypical temporal structure or rhythm, referred to as their 'temporal feature'.
source: Additionally, movement sequences are often characterized by a stereotypical temporal structure or rhythm—their 'temporal feature'.
evidence: This is a definitional claim establishing terminology used in the study.

claim: Temporal features can emerge spontaneously as part of chunk formation.
source: The latter can either emerge spontaneously as part of chunk formation (Sakai et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sakai et al., 2003.

claim: Temporal features can be directly relevant to the goal of the sequence, as in musical performance, dance, or speech.
source: or be directly relevant to the goal of the sequence, as in musical performance, dance, or speech (Shin and Ivry, 2002; Lewis and Miall, 2003; Repp, 2005; Kotz and Schwartze, 2010; Bläsing et al., 2012; Grahn, 2012; Penhune and Steele, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Experts can modify the temporal and spatial features of learned motor skills with ease.
source: One of the hallmarks of human motor performance is the ease with which experts can modify the temporal and spatial features of learned motor skills.
evidence: This is a general observation about expert motor performance based on established knowledge.

claim: A pianist is able to play the same tune using different variations of the rhythm.
source: For example, a pianist is able to play the same tune using different variations of the rhythm
evidence: This is an example illustrating flexibility in motor performance, based on common knowledge.

claim: A fluent speaker can change separately the word order or the rhythmic profile of speech for effective communication.
source: and a fluent speaker can change separately the word order or the rhythmic profile of speech for effective communication.
evidence: This is an example illustrating flexibility in motor performance, based on common knowledge.

claim: There has been a long-standing debate on whether a dedicated representation of temporal structure of skilled movements exists.
source: There has been a long-standing debate on whether a dedicated representation of temporal structure of skilled movements exists, or whether it is tightly integrated with a representation of its spatial features (Conditt and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1999; Shin and Ivry, 2002; Ullén and Bengtsson, 2003; Medina et al., 2005; Spencer and Ivry, 2009; Ali et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim references a scientific debate supported by multiple citations.

claim: Recent work suggests that spatio-temporal trajectories of movements can be learned and produced by a dynamical network of neurons that encodes patterned muscle dynamics.
source: Recent work suggests that spatio-temporal trajectories of movements can be learned and produced by a dynamical network of neurons that encodes patterned muscle dynamics, instead of by representing different parameters of a movement sequence separately (Laje and Buonomano, 2013; Shenoy et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent theoretical work.

claim: This neural implementation has been advocated for the primary motor and premotor cortices.
source: This neural implementation has been advocated for the primary motor and premotor cortices and implies that temporal features are stored inseparably from the specific movement trajectory trained.
evidence: This claim references theoretical proposals about motor cortex function.

claim: From the dynamical systems perspective, a spatial sequence performed with two different temporal profiles would constitute two distinct behaviours and demand the training of independent neural generators.
source: From this perspective, a spatial sequence performed with two different temporal profiles would constitute two distinct behaviours and demand the training of independent neural generators.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the dynamical systems theory described.

claim: The motor system may parse movement sequences into their constituent spatial and temporal features, which then are represented independently.
source: Alternatively, the motor system may parse movement sequences into their constituent spatial and temporal features, which then are represented independently.
evidence: This is a theoretical alternative hypothesis presented in the introduction.

claim: Independent encoding of spatial and temporal features would explain the ability of both animals and humans to flexibly recombine learned temporal patterns with a new spatial sequence and vice versa.
source: Such an encoding scheme would explain the ability of both animals and humans to flexibly recombine learned temporal patterns with a new spatial sequence and vice versa (Ullén and Bengtsson, 2003; Ali et al., 2013; Kornysheva et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies and logical inference.

claim: Neurons in the supplementary motor area (SMA) vary their firing rate for specific movement transitions and whole sequences of movements rather than for individual movements in a sequence.
source: For example, neurons in the supplementary motor area (SMA) vary their firing rate for specific movement transitions and whole sequences of movements rather than for individual movements in a sequence (Tanji and Shima, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to neurophysiological research.

claim: Inactivating the SMA, the primary motor cortex, the putamen or the dentate nucleus in monkeys disrupts sequential behaviour whilst sparing individual actions.
source: Inactivating the SMA, the primary motor cortex, the putamen or the dentate nucleus in monkeys disrupts sequential behaviour whilst sparing individual actions (Tanji and Shima, 1994; Shima and Tanji, 1998; Hikosaka et al., 1999; Lu and Ashe, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to inactivation studies in monkeys.

claim: A similar effect to monkey inactivation studies has been demonstrated for the SMA/pre-SMA in humans with non-invasive stimulation techniques.
source: with a similar effect demonstrated for the SMA/pre-SMA in humans with non-invasive stimulation techniques (Gerloff et al., 1997; Kennerley et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human stimulation studies.

claim: Recent evidence in primates argues for the existence of neurons tuned to specific temporal intervals between movements in the SMA, with a subset also tuned to the position of an interval in a sequence.
source: Recent evidence in primates also argues for the existence of neurons tuned to specific temporal intervals between movements in the same area, with a subset also tuned to the position of an interval in a sequence (Merchant et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent primate neurophysiology.

claim: It remains unknown whether neurons tuned to temporal intervals are simply part of a dynamical network that represents spatial and temporal features in an integrated manner, or whether independent populations of neurons encode spatial and temporal features in isolation.
source: However, it remains unknown whether these neurons are simply part of a dynamical network that represents spatial and temporal features in an integrated manner, or whether independent populations of neurons encode spatial and temporal features in isolation.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Specific neuronal sub-populations will become differentially active for different sequences following training.
source: We hypothesized that following training, specific neuronal sub-populations will become differentially active for different sequences, as has been observed in neurophysiological studies for spatial sequence features (Tanji and Shima, 1994).
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study supported by prior neurophysiological findings.

claim: If sequence-specific tuning is sufficiently clustered, it should be detectable with the relatively low spatial resolution of fMRI.
source: If such sequence-specific tuning is sufficiently clustered, it should be detectable with the relatively low spatial resolution of fMRI (Kamitani and Tong, 2005; Swisher et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on prior fMRI methodology studies showing detection of fine-grained patterns.

claim: A recent imaging study showed that sequential tuning can be detected in the human brain in a range of motor and premotor areas using a classification approach.
source: Using a classification approach to evaluate these subtle differences in the local patterns of brain activity during sequence production, a recent imaging study (Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013) indeed showed that such sequential tuning can be detected in the human brain in a range of motor and premotor areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior imaging study.

claim: The Wiestler and Diedrichsen 2013 study did not reveal whether and how motor areas represented spatial or temporal features of sequences.
source: This study, however, did not reveal whether and how these areas represented spatial or temporal features of sequences.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of prior work that the current study addresses.

claim: Participants were trained on nine sequences consisting of unique combinations of three spatial and three temporal features.
source: Participants were trained on nine sequences consisting of unique combinations of three spatial and three temporal features (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design, supported by the figure showing the sequence structure.

claim: Half the participants were trained on the right and half on the left hand.
source: Half the participants were trained on the right and half on the left hand to probe whether possible differences between hemispheres reflected hemispheric specialisation or the difference between contra vs ipsilateral encoding.
evidence: This describes the experimental design to control for hemispheric effects.

claim: Behavioural results show transfer of trained temporal and spatial features to new combinations.
source: First, by looking at behavioural generalisation, we show transfer of trained temporal and spatial features to new combinations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral transfer results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The average reaction time (RT) decreased from 410 ms (SD: 70) to 288 ms (SD: 48) over the course of 3 days of training.
source: The average reaction time (RT) decreased from 410 ms (SD: 70) to 288 ms (SD: 48, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct report of measured behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Subjects reduced the RT for untrained sequences from 456 ms (SD: 90) to 346 ms (SD: 64).
source: Subjects also reduced the RT for untrained sequences from 456 ms (SD: 90) to 346 ms (SD: 64), which suggests a general effect of visuomotor learning.
evidence: This is a direct report of measured behavioral data.

claim: The RT reduction for untrained sequences was significantly smaller than that for the trained sequences (F(1,30) = 13.342, p=0.001).
source: However, the reduction was significantly smaller than that for the trained sequences (F(1,30) = 13.342, p=0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: There was no interaction between RT reduction and group (right-hand-trained vs left hand, F(1,30) = 1.235, p=0.275).
source: and there was no interaction with the group (right-hand-trained vs left hand, F(1,30) = 1.235, p=0.275).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no difference between training groups.

claim: For trained sequences the error rate reduced from 46.1% (SD: 26.7) to 6.3% (SD: 4.9).
source: For trained sequences the error rate reduced from 46.1% (SD: 26.7) to 6.3% (SD: 4.9).
evidence: This is a direct report of measured behavioral data.

claim: For untrained sequences the error rate reduced from 52.1% (SD: 31.6) to 29.5% (SD: 21).
source: For untrained from 52.1% (SD: 31.6) to 29.5% (SD: 21), suggesting that the RT findings were not due to a change in the speed-accuracy trade-off.
evidence: This is a direct report of measured behavioral data with interpretation.

claim: The RTs increased during the fMRI session as compared to the end of training (t(31) = 6.57, p<0.0001).
source: The RTs increased as compared to the end of training (Figure 2B, t(31) = 6.57, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing RTs between training and fMRI sessions.

claim: Individual RTs during fMRI session strongly correlated with RTs for trained sequences in the last training block (r = 0.717, p<0.0001).
source: Importantly, however, across subjects individual RTs during fMRI session strongly correlated with RTs for trained sequences in the last training block (r = 0.717, p<0.0001), indicating that the responses reflected consistent measures of behaviour.
evidence: This is a statistical correlation result from the behavioral data.

claim: Repeating sequences nine times in the test phase yielded an immediate RT decrease for trained spatial sequences relative to untrained sequences.
source: Left panel: repeating sequences nine times in the test phase yielded an immediate RT decrease for trained spatial sequences (blue) relative to untrained sequences (black)
evidence: This describes results from the post-test shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only delayed RT differences were observed for trained temporal sequences in the post-test.
source: and only delayed RT differences for trained temporal sequences (red), in line with previous results (Kornysheva et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes results from the post-test with reference to prior work.

claim: Post-test results revealed significant RT advantages for the trained sequence, as well as the trained spatial and trained temporal feature conditions when compared to untrained sequences.
source: Right panel: a boxplot displaying RT results across subjects and all sequence repetitions in the post-test revealed significant RT advantages for the trained sequence, as well as the trained spatial and trained temporal feature conditions when compared to untrained sequences
evidence: This summarizes the statistical results from the post-test shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both the finger order and their relative timing were represented independently.
source: suggesting that both the finger order and their relative timing were represented independently.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral transfer results.

claim: Sequences which combined a trained temporal feature with an untrained feature were performed faster than a repetition of a completely novel sequence (F(1,28) = 12.963, p=0.001).
source: Averaged over all nine repetitions in the post-test, sequences which combined a trained temporal (F(1,28) = 12.963, p=0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the post-test analysis.

claim: Sequences which combined a trained spatial feature with an untrained feature were performed faster than a repetition of a completely novel sequence (F(1,28) = 20.830, p=0.0001).
source: or spatial (F(1,28) = 20.830, p=0.0001) feature with an untrained feature were performed faster than a repetition of a completely novel sequence (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the post-test analysis.

claim: Training of timed finger sequences automatically results in independent storage of its spatial and temporal features.
source: This suggests that training of timed finger sequences automatically results in independent storage of its spatial and temporal features.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral transfer results.

claim: Transfer effects did not differ between the left and right-hand-trained groups (p>0.127).
source: ANOVAs also revealed that these effects did not differ between the left and right-hand-trained groups (p>0.127).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group differences.

claim: The temporal representation acts as a multiplicative go signal on a concrete spatial plan.
source: These results replicate earlier findings and can be explained by a model in which the temporal representation acts as a multiplicative go signal on a concrete spatial plan (Kornysheva et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citation to a prior model.

claim: Without a spatial expectation, temporal knowledge does not have an effect.
source: Thus, without a spatial expectation, temporal knowledge does not have an effect.
evidence: This is an inference from the model explaining the delayed temporal transfer.

claim: Temporal transfer cannot manifest itself immediately, but only after a plan for the next movement has been formed.
source: For this reason, temporal transfer cannot manifest itself immediately, but only after a plan for the next movement has been formed (Hikosaka et al., 1999; Penhune and Steele, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior work on motor planning.

claim: Visually cued production of trained finger sequences yielded increased activity in motor and visual areas compared to rest.
source: Compared to rest, the visually cued production of trained finger sequences yielded increased activity in motor and visual areas.
evidence: This describes the average activation results from fMRI.

claim: Increased activation was observed in the contralateral primary motor cortex (hand knob area of M1) extending into the dorsal premotor cortex (PMd).
source: increased activation was observed in the contralateral primary motor cortex (hand knob area of M1) extending into the dorsal premotor cortex (PMd)
evidence: This describes specific brain regions showing activation in fMRI.

claim: Increased activation was observed in the ipsilateral lobule V-VI of the cerebellum.
source: the ipsilateral lobule V-VI of the cerebellum
evidence: This describes a specific brain region showing activation in fMRI.

claim: Increased activation was observed in bilateral (pre) supplementary motor area (SMA/pre-SMA).
source: bilateral (pre) supplementary motor area (SMA/pre-SMA)
evidence: This describes specific brain regions showing activation in fMRI.

claim: Increased activation was observed in bilateral ventral premotor cortex (PMv).
source: bilateral ventral premotor cortex (PMv)
evidence: This describes specific brain regions showing activation in fMRI.

claim: Increased activation was observed in left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC).
source: left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC)
evidence: This describes a specific brain region showing activation in fMRI.

claim: Increased activation was observed in visual areas—left posterior precuneus and secondary visual cortex (V2), as well as right associative visual and occipito-temporal cortices.
source: and visual areas—left posterior precuneus and secondary visual cortex (V2), as well as right associative visual and occipito-temporal cortices.
evidence: This describes specific brain regions showing activation in fMRI.

claim: The overall classifier shows above-chance accuracy whenever there are any reliable differences between the nine activity patterns, independently of the underlying tuning functions.
source: As confirmed by simulations of voxel activity patterns (Figure 3E, black bar), this classifier shows above-chance accuracy whenever there are any reliable differences between the nine activity patterns, independently of the underlying tuning functions, and therefore can detect any sequence representation.
evidence: This is validated by simulation results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The overall classifier found significant above-chance classification accuracy in the hand knob area of the contralateral M1 extending into primary sensory area (S1), PMd and PMv.
source: We found significant above-chance classification accuracy in the hand knob area of the contralateral M1 extending into primary sensory area (S1), PMd and PMv
evidence: This describes the results of the overall classifier analysis.

claim: The overall classifier found significant above-chance classification accuracy in the contralateral anterior insula.
source: the contralateral anterior insula
evidence: This describes a result from the overall classifier analysis.

claim: The overall classifier found significant above-chance classification accuracy in the ipsilateral Lobules V–VI of the cerebellum.
source: the ipsilateral Lobules V–VI of the cerebellum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This describes a result from the overall classifier analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The overall classifier found significant above-chance classification accuracy in the bilateral SMA, superior parietal and extrastriate cortices.
source: the bilateral SMA, superior parietal and extrastriate cortices
evidence: This describes results from the overall classifier analysis.

claim: The overall classifier found significant above-chance classification accuracy in the ipsilateral medial M1, and inferior parietal cortex.
source: the ipsilateral medial M1, and inferior parietal cortex (Figure 4A; Table 1).
evidence: This describes results from the overall classifier analysis shown in Figure 4A and Table 1.

claim: The above threshold clusters were more widespread on the contralateral than on the ipsilateral side.
source: Overall, the above threshold clusters were more widespread on the contralateral than on the ipsilateral side.
evidence: This is an observation from the overall classifier results.

claim: The results were in line with regions found in an earlier study by Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013.
source: These results were in line with the regions found in an earlier study (Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013), which used faster finger sequences that were produced from memory.
evidence: This compares current results to a prior study.

claim: Similar encoding can be found for visually paced sequences involving longer temporal intervals between finger presses.
source: Thus, our results indicate that similar encoding can be found for visually paced sequences involving longer temporal intervals between finger presses.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the current results to prior work.

claim: The only region that carried integrated, non-additive encoding was the M1 (handknob area) contralateral to the hand involved in producing the sequences.
source: The only region that carried such integrated, non-additive encoding was the cortical output area—the M1 (handknob area) contralateral to the hand involved in producing the sequences (Figure 4B, green, Table 1).
evidence: This describes the result of the integrated classifier analysis shown in Figure 4B and Table 1.

claim: Mean integrated encoding reached only significant above chance level in the contralateral M1 (p=0.0005, Bonferroni correction at p=0.05/8=0.0063).
source: Mean integrated encoding reached only significant above chance level in the contralateral M1 (Figure 5, p=0.0005, Bonferroni correction at p=0.05/8=0.0063)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ROI analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Integrated encoding was not significant in any of the premotor regions (p>0.155).
source: but not in any of the premotor regions (p>0.155).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ROI analysis.

claim: Spatial classification accuracy was significantly above chance in the contralateral SMA, bilateral PMd, as well as superior and inferior parietal lobes.
source: Spatial classification accuracy was significantly above chance in the contralateral SMA, bilateral PMd, as well as superior and inferior parietal lobes (Table 1).
evidence: This describes results from the spatial classifier analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Clusters in bilateral PMd, contralateral SMA, ipsilateral PMv, anterior and posterior cingulate, and bilateral extrastriate visual areas were significant for temporal classification after correction for multiple tests.
source: Clusters in bilateral PMd, contralateral SMA, ipsilateral PMv, anterior and posterior cingulate, and bilateral extrastriate visual areas were significant after correction for multiple tests (Table 1).
evidence: This describes results from the temporal classifier analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: While contralateral M1 exhibits mostly integrated encoding of temporal and spatial sequence features, the two sequence components are represented independently in the bilateral premotor cortex.
source: These results suggest that while contralateral M1 exhibits mostly integrated encoding of temporal and spatial sequence features, the two sequence components are represented independently in the bilateral premotor cortex.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the classification results.

claim: An ROI × hemisphere × classifier interaction was significant (F(1,30) = 12.808, p=0.001).
source: An ROI (M1 vs premotor) × hemisphere (contralateral vs ipsilateral) × classifier (integrated vs independent spatial and temporal) × group (right vs left hand) mixed ANOVA indeed revealed a significant ROI × hemisphere × classifier interaction (F(1,30) = 12.808, p=0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: The ROI × hemisphere × classifier interaction did not interact with group (p=0.75).
source: This effect did not interact with group (p=0.75)
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group differences.

claim: The distribution of integrated and independent sequence encoding was similar for left and right hand sequence production.
source: suggesting that although the effect was less pronounced for left-hand-trained participants, the distribution of integrated and independent sequence encoding was similar for left and right hand sequence production (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical results shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: A more caudal CoG was found for integrated, and a more rostral CoG for independent encoding in the contralateral hemispheres of both left- and right-hand groups.
source: Indeed, we found a more caudal CoG for integrated, and a more rostral CoG for independent encoding in the contralateral hemispheres of both left- and right-hand groups (Figure 6C).
evidence: This describes results from the center of gravity analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A hemisphere × classifier interaction was significant for the precentral CoG analysis (F(1,30) = 6.417, p=0.017).
source: A hemisphere (contralateral vs ipsilateral) × classifier (integrated vs independent) × group (right vs left hand) mixed ANOVA revealed a hemisphere × classifier interaction (F(1,30) = 6.417, p=0.017)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the CoG analysis.

claim: The hemisphere × classifier interaction did not interact with group for the precentral CoG (p=0.409).
source: but no interaction with group (p=0.409).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group differences.

claim: For the postcentral part of the cross-section, a more caudal CoG was found for independent as compared to integrated encoding.
source: For the postcentral part of the cross-section, we found the reverse pattern—a more caudal CoG for independent as compared to integrated encoding (Figure 6D).
evidence: This describes results from the CoG analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The hemisphere × classifier interaction was highly significant for the postcentral CoG (F(1,30) = 13.394, p=0.001).
source: Again the hemisphere (contralateral vs ipsilateral) × classifier (integrated vs independent) interaction was highly significant (F(1,30) = 13.394, p=0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the CoG analysis.

claim: The hemisphere × classifier interaction did not interact with group for the postcentral CoG (p=0.088).
source: and did not interact with group (p=0.088).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group differences.

claim: There is a difference in how primary motor and premotor, as well as parietal areas represent spatio-temporal finger sequences.
source: These results therefore clearly suggest a difference in how primary motor and premotor, as well as parietal areas represent spatio-temporal finger sequences.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the CoG analysis results.

claim: Temporal and spatial features were represented independently in premotor and parietal cortex.
source: Although temporal and spatial features were represented independently in premotor and parietal cortex (i.e., these regions showed specific activity patterns for one feature, independent of the respective other feature), spatially these representations overlapped to a certain degree, especially in caudal PMd (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes the pattern of results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Temporal encoding was more pronounced in the ventral premotor cortex, whereas spatial representations are more evident in the dorsal premotor cortex in the ipsilateral hemisphere.
source: Especially in the ipsilateral premotor cortex, it appears that temporal encoding was more pronounced in the ventral, whereas spatial representations are more evident in the dorsal premotor cortex.
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial distribution of classification results.

claim: A CoG across lateral premotor cortex revealed that temporal encoding was centred more ventrally and spatial encoding more dorsally.
source: A CoG across lateral premotor cortex indeed revealed that temporal encoding was centred more ventrally and spatial encoding more dorsally (Figure 6E).
evidence: This describes results from the CoG analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A main difference between temporal and spatial classifiers was found in the lateral premotor CoG analysis (F(1,30) = 5.836, p=0.022).
source: A hemisphere (contralateral vs ipsilateral) × classifier (temporal vs spatial) × group (right hand trained vs left hand) mixed ANOVA showed a main difference between classifier (F(1,30) = 5.836, p=0.022)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the CoG analysis.

claim: The classifier difference in lateral premotor CoG did not interact with group (p=0.687) or hemisphere (p=0.678).
source: but no interaction with group (p=0.687) or hemisphere (p=0.678).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no interactions.

claim: Outside of primary motor cortex, both temporal and spatial features of a learned movement sequence are represented independently, albeit in partly overlapping areas.
source: In summary, we found that outside of primary motor cortex, both temporal and spatial features of a learned movement sequence are represented independently, albeit in partly overlapping areas.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the classification analyses.

claim: There is a functional gradient with temporal representation being stronger in ventral and spatial representation stronger in dorsal premotor areas.
source: Furthermore, we found a functional gradient with temporal representation being stronger in ventral and spatial representation stronger in dorsal premotor areas.
evidence: This is a summary of the gradient findings from the CoG analysis.

claim: If the classification reflected tuning to individual finger movements, all classifiers should show the highest accuracy in the contralateral hand area of S1 and M1, where finger representations are the strongest.
source: First, if the classification reflected tuning to individual finger movements, all classifiers should show the highest accuracy in the contralateral hand area of S1 and M1, where finger representations are the strongest (Wiestler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a logical argument supported by citation to prior work on finger representations.

claim: A differential distribution of temporal, spatial, and integrated encoding across the brain was observed, which cannot be explained by finger tuning alone.
source: This, however, could not be observed, as evidenced by a differential distribution of temporal, spatial, and integrated encoding across the brain.
evidence: This is an observation from the results that argues against a simple finger tuning explanation.

claim: Each sequence trial was produced three times in a row (mini-block), so that the main response function was elevated across the execution of three sequences and did not return to baseline before the end of the last trial.
source: Second, each sequence trial was produced three times in a row (mini-block), so that the main response function was elevated across the execution of three sequences and did not return to baseline before the end of the last trial (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The main response function should be insensitive to differences in the temporal activation profile within each execution.
source: It therefore should be insensitive to differences in the temporal activation profile within each execution.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the design of the response function.

claim: The temporal derivative of the main response function captured variations of the temporal profile within each trial.
source: In contrast, the temporal derivative of the main response function included in our first level general linear model (GLM), captured variations of the temporal profile within each trial.
evidence: This describes the GLM design and what the derivative captures.

claim: Based on the derivative, increased classification accuracy of independent spatial and to some degree also temporal features was observed in M1.
source: As expected, based on the derivative, we observed increased classification accuracy of independent spatial and to some degree also temporal features in M1
evidence: This describes results from the derivative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In premotor areas such as the PMd, the independent classifiers performed much worse based on the derivative, in line with evidence suggesting weaker finger representations in premotor areas.
source: while in premotor areas such as the PMd, the independent classifiers performed much worse, in line with the evidence suggesting weaker finger representations in premotor areas (Diedrichsen et al., 2013b).
evidence: This describes results from the derivative analysis with reference to prior work.

claim: The factors response type, ROI, and hemisphere showed a significant three-way interaction for spatial encoding (F(1,31) = 9.165, p=0.005).
source: The factors response type (main response vs derivative), ROI (M1 vs PMd), and hemisphere (contralateral vs ipsilateral) showed a significant interaction between the three factors for both spatial (F(1,31) = 9.165, p=0.005)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the derivative analysis.

claim: The factors response type, ROI, and hemisphere showed a significant three-way interaction for temporal encoding (F(1,31) = 5.395, p=0.027).
source: and temporal encoding (F(1,31) = 5.395, p=0.027).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the derivative analysis.

claim: The voxel patterns based on the main response estimates are unlikely to reflect differences in the temporal profile of the observed response.
source: This suggests that the voxel patterns based on the main response estimates are unlikely to reflect differences in the temporal profile of the observed response.
evidence: This is an inference from the derivative analysis results.

claim: In some subjects minor, but systematic finger force differences between the trained sequences occurred.
source: Despite employing the same fingers and the same temporal intervals across all nine sequences, as well as by controlling the number of runs and jumps between finger digits and intervals (ascending or descending interval transitions), in some subjects minor, but systematic finger force differences between the trained sequences occurred, such as more force on the thumb in one sequence and on the index finger in a different sequence (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes observed force differences shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Force on the five fingers could be used to reliably classify the nine-trained sequences (mean zacc = 2.25, t(31) = 10.914, p<0.001).
source: Accordingly, force on the five fingers could be used to reliably classify the nine-trained sequences (mean zacc = 2.25, t(31) = 10.914, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the force classification analysis.

claim: The strength of force differences did not correlate with classification accuracy in contralateral M1 (r = −0.210, p=0.257).
source: Importantly, however, the strength of force differences did not correlate with classification accuracy in contralateral M1 (r = −0.210, p=0.257)
evidence: This is a correlation result showing no relationship between force and classification.

claim: Simple differences in finger forces could not account for the finding of integrated feature encoding in M1.
source: such that simple differences in finger forces could not account for the finding of integrated feature encoding here.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of correlation between force and classification.

claim: The classification accuracy in contralateral M1 correlated with the amount of sequence-specific learning (r = 0.468, p=0.008).
source: Indeed, the classification accuracy correlated with the amount of sequence-specific learning, (r = 0.468, p=0.008).
evidence: This is a correlation result shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Participants with higher behavioural learning effects also showed higher classification accuracy in contralateral M1.
source: Thus, participants with higher behavioural learning effects also showed higher classification accuracy (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation result shown in Figure 7A.

claim: No positive relationship could be revealed for ipsilateral M1 and either force differences or sequence learning (r <−0.222, p>0.186).
source: No positive relationship could be revealed for ipsilateral M1 and either force differences or sequence learning (r <−0.222, p>0.186, Figure 7B for correlation with sequence learning).
evidence: This is a correlation result shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Encoding in contralateral M1 is likely to be related to the sequential skill level.
source: This further supports that encoding in contralateral M1 is likely to be related to the sequential skill level.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between classification and learning.

claim: The integrated sequence encoding found in the contralateral M1 is in line with electrophysiological data showing that 40% of neurons in the primary motor area in monkeys can exhibit tuning to sequences of muscle commands.
source: The integrated sequence encoding found in the contralateral M1 is in line with electrophysiological data showing that 40% of neurons in the primary motor area in monkeys can exhibit tuning to sequences of muscle commands (Matsuzaka et al., 2007)
evidence: This relates the current findings to prior electrophysiological work via citation.

claim: Inactivation of M1 via muscimol can selectively disrupt sequential behaviour.
source: evidence that inactivation of M1 via muscimol can selectively disrupt sequential behaviour (Lu and Ashe, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to an inactivation study.

claim: The overall sequence encoding in the contralateral M1 covaried with the amount of behavioural advantages for the trained sequences.
source: We found that the overall sequence encoding in the contralateral M1 covaried with the amount of behavioural advantages for the trained sequences
evidence: This is a correlation result relating neural and behavioral measures.

claim: The analysis uncovered skill-dependent representations in M1.
source: suggesting that our analysis uncovered skill-dependent representations.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between encoding and learning.

claim: Each spatio-temporal sequence combination having its unique activity pattern in M1 is consistent with a dynamical systems view.
source: The fact that each spatio-temporal sequence combination had its unique activity pattern in M1 is consistent with a dynamical systems view which proposes that each movement is controlled by a subpopulation of neurons that form a dynamical network (Laje and Buonomano, 2013; Shenoy et al., 2013).
evidence: This relates the findings to dynamical systems theory via citations.

claim: For each unique spatio-temporal sequence a slightly different distribution of neurons is activated in M1 which in turn cause distinct voxel activity patterns.
source: Accordingly, for each unique spatio-temporal sequence a slightly different distribution of neurons is activated in M1 which in turn cause distinct voxel activity patterns for each of the studied sequence combinations (Kamitani and Tong, 2005; Kriegeskorte et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citations to fMRI methodology.

claim: The integrated encoding in M1 is in line with a model suggesting that temporal and spatial sequence features are integrated non-linearly in the nervous system.
source: This integrated encoding in M1 is in line with our model, which suggests that the temporal and spatial sequence features are integrated non-linearly in the nervous system (Kornysheva et al., 2013).
evidence: This relates the findings to a prior model via citation.

claim: Integrated encoding such as found in M1 alone would not allow the system to use learned spatial or temporal features independently.
source: While adequate for learning and producing specific spatio-temporal sequences, integrated encoding such as found in M1 alone would not allow the system to use learned spatial or temporal features independently.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional implications of integrated encoding.

claim: Subjects showed behavioural advantages for untrained sequences in which only one of the trained features (spatial or temporal) was retained.
source: However, subjects showed behavioural advantages for untrained sequence in which only one of the trained features (spatial or temporal) was retained.
evidence: This summarizes the behavioral transfer results.

claim: An integrated representation as proposed in dynamical systems models cannot explain the flexible transfer or independent adaptation of spatial and temporal features.
source: With spatial and temporal features of movement trajectories emerging from the same local circuits, an integrated representation as proposed in dynamical systems models (Shenoy et al., 2013) cannot explain the flexible transfer or independent adaptation of spatial and temporal features reported here and in previous studies (Ullén and Bengtsson, 2003; Ali et al., 2013; Kornysheva et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a logical argument against dynamical systems models based on the current and prior results.

claim: Higher order motor areas (lateral and medial premotor cortices) parsed the sequences into the two constituent features.
source: In contrast, our results indicate that higher order motor areas (lateral and medial premotor cortices) parsed the sequences into the two constituent features, in line with the modularity and flexibility we observed in behaviour.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging results in relation to behavior.

claim: The independent albeit partly overlapping spatial and temporal encoding suggests a modular feature-separating storage for movement production.
source: The independent albeit partly overlapping spatial and temporal encoding suggests a modular feature-separating storage for movement production.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging results.

claim: It is possible that not all classes of movements lend themselves to separation of temporal and spatial features.
source: Although our experiment provides both behavioural and imaging evidence for the independent representation of temporal and spatial features of movements, it is possible that not all classes of movements lend themselves to such a separation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: The temporal profile of a force perturbation during a reaching movement is learned inseparably from the whole spatio-temporal trajectory.
source: For example, the temporal profile of a force perturbation during a reaching movement is learned inseparably from the whole spatio-temporal trajectory (Conditt and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study on reaching movements.

claim: One critical factor that distinguishes classes of movements may be whether movement kinematics are continuous or fall into discrete phases.
source: One critical factor that distinguishes these classes may be whether movement kinematics are continuous as in reaching movements or fall into discrete phases, as induced by the current task (Ivry et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a theoretical speculation supported by citation.

claim: For discrete sequential movements, the evidence for an independent representation of the temporal structure is compelling.
source: In contrast, for discrete sequential movements, as studied here, the evidence for an independent representation of the temporal structure is compelling.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the strength of evidence for the current findings.

claim: The behavioral finding is unlikely to be an effect artificially induced by the orthogonal design.
source: Importantly, our behavioural finding is unlikely to be an effect artificially induced by the orthogonal design, in which all three spatial sequence features were crossed with three temporal features, since flexibility in independently adapting spatial or temporal features of sequences has also been observed in a previous study which involved the training of only one particular spatio-temporal combination (Kornysheva et al., 2013).
evidence: This argues against a design artifact by citing a prior study with different design.

claim: Previous data demonstrated that the premotor cortex modulates its activity once movement sequences are made more complex in either their spatial or temporal structure.
source: Previous data demonstrated that the premotor cortex modulates its activity once movement sequences are made more complex in either their spatial or temporal structure (Bengtsson et al., 2004), or in the presence of both features (Sakai et al., 2002; Brown et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior imaging studies.

claim: Previous studies did not establish how temporal and spatial features were encoded in premotor cortex.
source: However, these studies did not establish how temporal and spatial features were encoded.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of prior work.

claim: A recent study showed that voxel pattern analysis can uncover sequence representations in motor and premotor areas, which are specifically enhanced for trained sequences.
source: Here, we address this issue, starting from a recent study that showed that voxel pattern analysis can uncover sequence representations in motor and premotor areas, which are specifically enhanced for trained sequences (Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior methodological study.

claim: The representational analysis allowed distinguishing between integrated vs independent representations, even if the independent spatial and temporal representations overlapped spatially.
source: Our representational analysis allowed us for the first time to distinguish between integrated vs independent representations, even if the independent spatial and temporal representations overlapped spatially.
evidence: This describes the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The analysis hinges critically on the assumption that activity in independent neuronal populations within a single voxel combine additively in the observed BOLD signal.
source: While we validated this approach by voxel pattern simulations, the analysis hinges critically on the assumption that activity in independent neuronal populations within a single voxel combine additively in the observed BOLD signal.
evidence: This states a key assumption of the analysis method.

claim: Functional imaging signals show clear non-linearities when studied over a large dynamic range.
source: Functional imaging signals show clear non-linearities when studied over a large dynamic range (Logothetis et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior fMRI methodology work.

claim: The activity of single voxels only varied very slightly between different sequences in the current paradigm.
source: However, the activity of single voxels only varied very slightly between different sequences in our paradigm.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the current data.

claim: For the restricted range of activity variation, a linear approximation is reasonable.
source: For this restricted range, therefore, we can be relatively confident that a linear approximation is reasonable (Diedrichsen et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by citation.

claim: Any non-linearity between neural signal and hemodynamic response should be relatively homogenous across adjacent cortical motor areas.
source: Furthermore, because any non-linearity between neural signal and hemodynamic response should be relatively homogenous across adjacent cortical motor areas, the distinct representational dissociation found between M1 and PMd is likely to reflect neural rather than hemodynamic differences.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the interpretation of the results.

claim: Neurons in primate premotor cortices have been shown to be tuned to specific spatial transitions between movement elements and whole sequences of movements.
source: Neurons in primate premotor cortices have been shown to be tuned to specific spatial transitions between movement elements and whole sequences of movements increasing their firing rate prior to a movement based on its sequential context (Mushiake et al., 1991; Tanji and Shima, 1994; Shima and Tanji, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to primate neurophysiology studies.

claim: Such units have been suggested to be an important component in the organisation of skilled sequential behaviours.
source: Such units have been suggested to be an important component in the organisation of skilled sequential behaviours
evidence: This references theoretical proposals about the function of these neurons.

claim: Whether timing between movements modulates the same neurons that encode spatial sequences has not been systematically explored.
source: however whether timing between movements modulates the same neurons has not been systematically explored.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the neurophysiological literature.

claim: The findings of independent representations predict that the representation of movement order in space first reported by Shima and Tanji in the SMA is likely to be independent of the exact timing of individual movements in the sequence.
source: Our findings of independent representations of the spatial and temporal features predict that the representation of movement order in space first reported by Shima and Tanji in the SMA (Tanji and Shima, 1994) is likely to be independent of the exact timing of individual movements in the sequence.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the current findings and prior neurophysiology.

claim: Changing the temporal intervals between movements in a sequence should not interfere with the tuning of a neuron to a specific spatial movement transition or sequence.
source: In other words, changing the temporal intervals between movements in a sequence should not interfere with the tuning of the neuron to a specific spatial movement transition or sequence.
evidence: This is a specific prediction about single neuron responses based on the current findings.

claim: The findings predict independent encoding of the temporal features of movement sequences within the same areas as the spatial features.
source: At the same time our findings predict independent encoding of the temporal features of movement sequences within the same areas as the spatial features.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the current findings.

claim: Merchant et al. (2013) found evidence for the encoding of sub-second intervals sensitive to the sequential context within a synchronization-continuation task in the medial premotor cortex of monkeys.
source: In the medial premotor cortex of monkeys, Merchant et al. (2013) found evidence for the encoding of sub-second intervals sensitive to the sequential context within a synchronization-continuation task.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a primate neurophysiology study.

claim: Merchant et al. found cells that are tuned to both a specific interval between movements and a specific position in a sequence.
source: In addition to neurons tuned to interval duration, the authors found cells that are tuned to both a specific interval between movements and a specific position in a sequence, for example, a neuron increased its firing rate only to the 850 ms interval between the fifth and sixth lever push.
evidence: This describes specific findings from the Merchant et al. study.

claim: The type of encoding found by Merchant et al. would be detectable with the current method since in the trained sequences the individual digits and temporal intervals occurred at unique positions.
source: This type of encoding would be detectable with our method since in the trained sequences the individual digits and temporal intervals occurred at unique positions.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about what the current approach can detect.

claim: It is currently unknown whether the type of encoding found by Merchant et al. would generalize to a sequential temporal pattern similar to the one employed in the current task.
source: However, the intervals tested in each sequence were isochronous, and it is currently unknown whether this type of encoding would generalize to a sequential temporal pattern similar to the one employed in the current task.
evidence: This identifies a limitation in relating the current findings to prior neurophysiology.

claim: The timing of motor responses can be related to the firing of neural units in the cerebellum, as in the case of cerebellar Purkinje cells which decrease simple spike activity in a timed fashion.
source: Furthermore, the timing of a motor responses can be related to the firing of neural units in the cerebellum, as for instance in the case of cerebellar Purkinje cells which decrease simple spike activity in a timed fashion depending on the trained interval between the conditioning stimulus and the conditioned response following training (Jirenhed and Hesslow, 2011a, 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cerebellar neurophysiology studies.

claim: Whether cerebellar timing encoding can also be modulated by the sequential context is not known.
source: Yet, whether this type of encoding can also be modulated by the sequential context is not known.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge about cerebellar function.

claim: The cerebellum did not yield significant results with regard to temporal encoding.
source: In contrast to our findings in the cortex, the cerebellum did not yield significant results with regard to temporal encoding
evidence: This describes a null result in the cerebellum.

claim: There was a clear significant overall encoding of the sequences in the ipsilateral lobule VI of the cerebellum.
source: although there was a clear significant overall encoding of the sequences in the ipsilateral lobule VI which forms reciprocal connections with contralateral premotor areas (Buckner et al., 2011; Bostan et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes a positive result in the cerebellum supported by anatomical citations.

claim: The cerebellar null result for temporal encoding could be related to higher noise levels for subtentorial structures.
source: This null result could be related to higher noise levels for subtentorial structures (Wiestler et al., 2011)
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the null result supported by citation.

claim: The cerebellar null result for temporal encoding could be related to the more complex folding structure of the cerebellar cortex, which may push the informative signal variations below the threshold of effective spatial resolution.
source: or the more complex folding structure of the cerebellar cortex, which may push the informative signal variations below the threshold of effective spatial resolution.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the null result based on anatomical considerations.

claim: A gradient was found with spatial features represented more in dorsal and temporal features more in ventral aspects of the lateral premotor cortex, similar to studies involving spatial and temporal production.
source: Despite partly overlapping temporal and spatial representations, we found a gradient with spatial features represented more in dorsal and temporal features more in ventral aspects of the lateral premotor cortex similar to studies involving spatial and temporal production (Bengtsson et al., 2004) and prediction (Schubotz and von Cramon, 2001).
evidence: This describes a gradient in the results with reference to prior studies.

claim: The regional distribution raises the possibility that the temporal representation may not be an abstract representation of the temporal structure of sequences, but rather a representation of an additional effector system.
source: This regional distribution raises the possibility that the temporal representation uncovered here may not be an abstract representation of the temporal structure of sequences, but rather a representation of an additional effector system.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the gradient findings.

claim: Most subjects' introspective reports suggest subvocal rehearsal at the beginning of their training, albeit less so towards the end of training and during fMRI.
source: Indeed, most subjects' introspective reports suggests subvocal rehearsal at the beginning of their training, albeit less so towards the end of training and during fMRI.
evidence: This reports subjective data from participants.

claim: A simple mapping of the temporal feature representations to the control of vocal sequencing and timing is unlikely.
source: However, a simple mapping of the temporal feature representations to the control of vocal sequencing and timing is unlikely.
evidence: This is an argument against a simple vocal explanation based on anatomical considerations.

claim: There was no direct involvement of more posterior and perisylvian primary vocalization centres in temporal encoding.
source: There was no direct involvement of more posterior and perisylvian primary vocalization centres.
evidence: This describes the absence of activation in vocal areas.

claim: Temporal encoding largely overlapped with spatial encoding along the premotor cortex, instead of being restricted to ventral-most premotor areas recruited for rhythmically structured vocal rehearsal.
source: Moreover, cross-sections through the cortical Brodmann area 6 suggest that temporal encoding largely overlapped with spatial encoding along the premotor cortex, instead of being restricted to ventral-most premotor areas recruited for rhythmically structured vocal rehearsal (Riecker et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the spatial distribution of encoding with reference to vocal areas.

claim: The nervous system may build on specialised processes in premotor areas for temporal control, which have originally evolved for the sequencing of the oro-facial and laryngeal musculature in speech production.
source: Instead, the nervous system may build on specialised processes in premotor areas for temporal control, which have originally evolved for the sequencing of the oro-facial and laryngeal musculature in speech production (Schubotz, 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation supported by citation.

claim: A temporal representation in the premotor cortex could modulate the finger motor system at the level of M1 by interacting with premotor input from the spatial representation in a non-linear manner.
source: Such a temporal representation in the premotor cortex could modulate the finger motor system at the level of M1 by interacting with premotor input from the spatial representation in a non-linear manner, as suggested in our multiplicative model (Kornysheva et al., 2013), thereby modulating the integrated dynamical systems representation of the sequences in M1.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation linking the findings to a prior model.

claim: The presence of multiple temporal and spatial representations across the cortex suggests parallel computations related to the same sequential features.
source: The presence of multiple temporal and spatial representations across the cortex suggests parallel computations related to the same sequential features.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the distributed representations found.

claim: Multiple representations may have complimentary functions.
source: These may have complimentary functions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of multiple representations.

claim: The medial vs lateral premotor cortex encoding of sequence features may be related to the concurrent encoding of both internally and externally (visually) driven sequential movements.
source: The medial vs lateral premotor cortex encoding of sequence features may be related to the concurrent encoding of both internally and externally (visually) driven sequential movements (Goldberg, 1985; Mushiake et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Within the lateral premotor cortex, temporal processing has been hypothesized to be associated with the degree of motor involvement.
source: Within the lateral premotor cortex, temporal processing has been hypothesized to be associated with the degree of motor involvement
evidence: This references a theoretical hypothesis about premotor function.

claim: Chen et al. (2009) showed that the ventral premotor cortex enables direct action-related encoding of temporal structure while the dorsal premotor cortex facilitates higher order temporal organisation of sequences.
source: Chen et al. (2009) have shown that the ventral premotor cortex enables direct action-related encoding of temporal structure while the dorsal premotor cortex facilitates higher order temporal organisation of sequences, in line with the direct vs indirect transformation hypothesis by Hoshi and Tanji (2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on premotor function.

claim: Multiple spatial representations may reflect different spatial sequence reference frames.
source: Finally, multiple spatial representations may reflect different spatial sequence reference frames—such as movement sequences in extrinsic spatial coordinates in the rostral PMd and the posterior parietal cortex (Brown et al., 2013; Wiestler et al., 2014) and in intrinsic spatial coordinates in the caudal PMd (Wiestler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior work on reference frames.

claim: A diversity of spatial and temporal sequence representations across the network of premotor and parietal areas may enable flexible control of skilled behaviour that can adapt to the situational task requirements.
source: Taken together, such a diversity of spatial and temporal sequence representations across the network of premotor and parietal areas may enable flexible control of skilled behaviour that can adapt to the situational task requirements.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation of the distributed representations.

claim: The independent encoding of the spatial and temporal features of movement sequences in premotor areas endows the nervous system with the ability for adjustments of individual movement parameters.
source: Overall, the independent encoding of the spatial and temporal features of movement sequences in premotor areas endows the nervous system with the ability for adjustments of individual movement parameters—which would not be possible with a fixed integrated representation such as in M1 alone.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the independent encoding findings.

claim: Separate encoding may explain why a pianist who learned a particular passage can effortlessly produce the same sequence of finger movements with a novel rhythmic structure.
source: For example, this separate encoding may explain why a pianist who learned a particular passage can effortlessly produce the same sequence of finger movements with a novel rhythmic structure—or combine the same rhythm with new variations of the sequence of notes.
evidence: This is an example illustrating the functional implications of independent encoding.

claim: The decomposition into features in the premotor cortex provides a computational solution for representing longer and more complex sequences of actions.
source: Finally, the decomposition into features in the premotor cortex provides a computational solution for representing longer and more complex sequences of actions.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the computational advantage of feature decomposition.

claim: If the system utilized integrated encoding alone, it would have to represent all relevant permutations of spatial, temporal and other relevant parameters, which very quickly would lead to a combinatorial explosion.
source: If the system utilized integrated encoding alone, such as in the primary motor cortex, it would have to represent all relevant permutations of spatial, temporal and other relevant parameters (e.g., amplitude and direction), which very quickly would lead to a combinatorial explosion.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the computational limitations of integrated encoding.

claim: The premotor cortex may dedicate its resources to representing features separately, creating a more compact and flexible representation.
source: Instead, the premotor cortex may dedicate its resources to representing these features separately, creating a more compact and flexible representation.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the computational advantage of premotor encoding.

claim: This architecture has parallels in the ventral visual stream, in which lower visual areas encode specific combinations of simple features at specific spatial locations, whereas higher visual areas represent more complex visual arrangements independently of their orientation or location.
source: This special feature may explain why evolution endowed us with premotor areas, rather than simply with a larger primary motor cortex. This architecture has parallels in the ventral visual stream, in which lower visual areas encode specific combinations of simple features at specific spatial locations, whereas higher visual areas represent more complex visual arrangements—such as body parts and scenes—independently of their orientation or location of the stimulus (Freeman and Simoncelli, 2011).
evidence: This draws an analogy to the visual system supported by citation.

claim: The decomposition of movements into features may be the cardinal function of premotor areas.
source: Thus, the decomposition of movements into features may be the cardinal function of premotor areas
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion about premotor function based on the findings.

claim: Feature decomposition endows the system both with behavioural flexibility and the capacity to store long, complex sequences of movements.
source: and endow the system both with behavioural flexibility and the capacity to store long, complex sequences of movements.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the computational advantages of feature decomposition.

claim: 32 neurologically healthy volunteers participated in this study (16 female), aged between 19 and 36 (mean: 24.8, SD: 5.6).
source: 32 neurologically healthy volunteers took part in this study (16 female), aged between 19 and 36 (mean: 24.8, SD: 5.6).
evidence: This describes the participant demographics.

claim: All subjects were right-handed according to the Edinburgh Inventory of Manual Preference with a mean score of 89 (range: 70–100; SD: 11.9).
source: All subjects were right-handed according to the Edinburgh Inventory of Manual Preference (Oldfield, 1971) with a mean score of 89 (range: 70–100; SD: 11.9; both groups had the same mean score of 89, right group SD: 10.4, left group: SD 13.5).
evidence: This describes participant handedness with reference to a standard assessment.

claim: None of the participants were professional musicians or athletes.
source: None of them were professional musicians or athletes.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion for participants.

claim: All subjects were naive concerning the hypothesis of this study.
source: All subjects were naive concerning the hypothesis of this study.
evidence: This describes the blinding of participants to the study hypothesis.

claim: Experimental procedures were approved by the research ethics committee of University College London.
source: Experimental procedures were approved by the research ethics committee of University College London.
evidence: This describes ethical approval for the study.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from each participant for data analysis and publication of the study results.
source: Written informed consent was obtained from each participant for data analysis and publication of the study results.
evidence: This describes the consent process.
